messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata (10.1021/acsestwater.2c00660, https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestwater.2c00660).
Author list, title, journal, year, volume, and pages match the citation provided in the source text.

The methods section states that pilot-scale experiments were performed on PFAS-contaminated groundwater and landfill leachate at the Hovgården landfill and that EO was applied directly to the groundwater and leachate (S08-E07). This supports the description of PFAS-contaminated groundwater and landfill leachate at Hovgården treated directly by EO without preconcentration.

S08-E07 explicitly describes "Pilot-scale experiments" carried out on-site at the Hovgården landfill and notes EO was applied directly to groundwater and leachate as well as to collapsed foam. This supports the characterization as pilot-scale, on-site EO directly applied to bulk groundwater and landfill leachate without prior foam fractionation for that treatment configuration.

S08-E07 reports that EO was applied directly to the groundwater and leachate as well as to collapsed foam from the FF process, and the paper overall evaluates the FF–EO treatment train (also summarized in the abstract S08-E01). S08-E05 contrasts direct EO of all water with EO of foam in terms of degradation efficiencies and energy use. This supports the description of EO applied directly to the full contaminated volume without foam preconcentration and compared with an FF–EO train regarding degradation and energy implications.

S08-E07 notes that EO was applied directly to groundwater and leachate and to collapsed foam produced in on-site FF, and S08-E01 describes the FF–EO train, i.e., preconcentrated foam treated by EO. This supports the description of a treatment configuration contrasting direct EO of all contaminated water with EO of preconcentrated foam in the FF–EO train.
The operating condition is a categorical description of treatment configuration, so having no unit is appropriate and consistent with the source.

S08-E05 states that when treating all the water directly with EO, energy use was higher "due to the 10-fold larger volume requiring energy-intensive destructive treatment." This directly supports the numeric value 10 for the relative treated volume compared with the FF–EO train.
The source explicitly refers to a "10-fold" larger volume (S08-E05), so expressing the unit as "fold" is consistent with the text.

The qualifier text paraphrases S08-E05, which states that treating all the water directly with EO has higher energy use because of the 10-fold larger volume requiring energy-intensive destructive treatment.

The abstract (S08-E01) reports degradation of long- and short-chain PFAS, indicating a mixture of PFAS including both chain lengths. S08-E04 discusses normalized energy consumption per log removal of PFOA, showing that PFOA is used as a reference compound for energy metrics. Together these support the described PFAS scope.

S08-E05 explicitly refers to "degradation efficiencies" when comparing direct EO of all water with EO of fractionated foam. This indicates that the measured outcome is PFAS degradation/removal by EO, so classifying the endpoint_type as degradation is appropriate.

S08-E05 states that when treating all the water directly with EO, degradation efficiencies were higher but at the cost of higher energy use due to a 10-fold larger treated volume. The provided interpretation accurately reflects this comparison and notes that exact degradation percentages are not provided in the cited text, which is correct for the supplied excerpt.

The record’s reported term paraphrases the terminology in S08-E05, which discusses "degradation efficiencies" for direct EO versus the FF–EO configuration. This is an accurate reflection of the author language.

S08-E05 supports that treating all water directly with EO yields higher degradation efficiencies but requires a 10-fold larger volume of water to undergo energy-intensive destructive treatment, leading to higher energy use. However, the specific claim that this "questions the practicality for large-scale implementation" is an interpretive extrapolation not stated in the cited text. Thus, the core limitation (higher energy demand due to 10-fold volume) is supported, but the extended implication about practicality is not directly author-reported.

The underlying facts (higher degradation but 10-fold volume and higher energy use) are author-reported in S08-E05, but the framing as a limitation about practicality of large-scale implementation is added by the extractor and not explicitly stated by the authors. Therefore, the basis being purely author_reported is only partially supported.

S08-E08 notes low degradation of PFSA in fractionated foam and states this may be due to mass transfer or matrix-specific effects, recommending further mechanistic EO studies on foam. This supports the part of the statement about mass transfer limitations and matrix-specific effects influencing EO performance, particularly for PFSA. However, the claim that these factors "imply potential persistence of some PFAS in residual streams when EO is applied without prior concentration" extends beyond the cited text, which discusses foam (preconcentrated) EO, not direct EO without concentration. That extrapolation is not directly supported.

Mass transfer and matrix-specific effects on PFSA degradation are clearly author-reported (S08-E08), but the added implication about persistence in residual streams for direct EO without preconcentration is interpretive. Thus, labeling the entire statement as author_reported is only partially supported.

The status "descriptive_only" indicates that only qualitative comparison is possible. S08-E05 qualitatively compares higher degradation efficiencies for direct EO versus the FF–EO train but notes higher energy use due to a 10-fold larger treated volume; the supplied excerpts do not contain detailed operating parameters or comprehensive numeric metrics for both configurations. Given this limited quantitative detail in the cited text, the judgment that comparability is descriptive_only is reasonable and supported.

The reason cites that direct EO is qualitatively reported as having higher degradation but requires treating a much larger volume and more energy, while lacking detailed operating parameters and residual management metrics. S08-E05 supports the qualitative comparison and 10-fold volume, and the absence of detailed numerical comparison metrics in the provided excerpts justifies stating that quantitative comparison is limited.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix (PFAS-contaminated groundwater and landfill leachate at Hovgården), treatment configuration (direct EO vs FF–EO), scale (pilot-scale, on-site), and endpoint type (PFAS degradation)—are well supported by the cited text. Numeric operating information (10-fold treated volume) is correctly transcribed and unitized. Some interpretive extensions in the limitations and residuals/byproducts descriptions go beyond the cited language, but these are clearly non-core qualifiers and do not misrepresent the primary experimental conditions or outcomes. The record is therefore usable for synthesis, with caution to treat limitations and residual implications as partially supported interpretations rather than strict author statements.
